new_statements.translation: Accentuation: The orthographic accent, for the purposes of this Vocabulary, is written only on the stressed syllables of the roots of inflectable words, and on words of two and three syllables that are not paroxytone. The stress of the suffixes will be seen in the Appendix 'Grammatical Notes' and, since it is almost constant, it is not necessary to write it. The first stressed syllable of a word carries more force than the others, and is always one of the first two syllables of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words may carry more than one stressed syllable; the leftmost stressed syllable is the strongest (primary) and always falls on the first or second syllable of the word. Which of the two it is must be learned per root (hence the orthographic accent on roots), with the Spanish-style convention that unmarked 2-3-syllable words are paroxytone; suffix stress is nearly constant and not. Provisional reading: lexically placed primary stress within an initial two-syllable window (initial or peninitial).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied but not analysed: example words carry two written accents (chóró 'choro monkey', kápá 'thorn', máká 'snake', gópogó 'snail', dáraná 'lizard', p. 233); suffixes have their own 'almost constant' stress (p. 235); the first stressed syllable is stronger than the later ones.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphological shift: for n3-type noun roots the 3rd-person possessive form 'se cambia el acento principal a la primera sílaba del radical y se pierde la sílaba anteriormente acentuada' (main accent moves to the first syllable of the root and the previously accented syllable is lost) (p. 240). Vowel loss at unstressed morpheme junctures (p. 236).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('palabra'), stated as an orthographic convention for the dictionary's citation forms; distinguishes root stress from suffix stress (unwritten, nearly constant). Author is an SIL fieldworker; no phonetic/phonological analysis, no minimal pairs. The 2008 edition reprints the 1966 text.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuggy's Vocabulario describes 'Candoshi de Loreto', i.e. the Candoshi proper (Murato) rather than the Shapra (Chápara) of the Río Morona, whom Tuggy names as the other division of the same people (p. v); Glottolog has no separate code for Shapra, so the record belongs under cand1248 with the dialect flagged as Candoshi/Murato. Overall's 2023 chapter uses the name Kandozi-Chapra for the same language.

sources.note: Apéndice I 'Ortología' (pp. 232-236), paragraph 'Acentuación' p. 235: written accent marks the tonic syllables of roots and of 2-3-syllable words that are not paroxytone; suffix stress is 'casi constante' and unwritten; the first stressed syllable of a word is the strongest and is always one of the first two syllables. Example words on p. 233 carry several accents (chóró, kápá, gópogó, dáraná). Apéndice II p. 240: 3rd-person possessive of n3-type noun roots shifts the main accent to the first syllable of the root.
